Hojaiga: teaching a Windows assistant to learn any app and prove its work

Dhruv PatelAugust to November 2026107 commits · about 230k lines of Python · 29 test suites

Abstract

Hojaiga was an attempt to build a desktop assistant that is handed any Windows application, learns how it works on its own, and then carries out real tasks in it, reporting a task as done only when the result can be proven. Over twelve weeks it grew into a layered system: knowledge harvested from a program's own files, live interface mapping through UI Automation and vision, a background "virtual mouse" that never moves the person's cursor, object-model control of Office, a consequence gate for risky actions, and a proof step that reads back saved files or judges the final window. The structured layers worked where structure existed. The plan to make small local vision-language models (2 to 8 billion parameters on a 6 GB laptop GPU) the system's eyes and brain did not: a fine-tuned 4B model scored 39% on held-out tasks against 53% for the untouched base model, and self-directed practice proved 2 of 100 tasks. The final design keeps the verified, structured core and adds a teacher: a strong hosted model on the user's own API key proposes each step, a local "brain" checks it against the real controls on screen, keeps only proven steps, and turns the teacher off once it agrees often enough. This report records what was built, what was measured, what failed and why, and credits the work that shaped it, in particular Clicky by Farza.

1The idea and the business

The problem. Most automation needs a custom integration for every program: an API, a connector, a recorded script that breaks when a button moves. Much of the software people actually use has none of those, especially older Windows programs inside companies. People, on the other hand, open an unfamiliar app, look at it, try things, and get faster.

The product. Hojaiga was meant to be an "automation operating system" for Windows: hand it any application and it learns how that application works on its own, from the program's files and from its screen, then does real work in it in the background and proves the result before it says "done". It could also teach: point at the right button and explain what it does.

The niche. Four things together set it apart from what I could find:

  • Windows-native and any app: desktop programs, Office, browsers and old line-of-business tools, with no per-app code.
  • Own intelligence, on the person's machine: local models and local knowledge, no paid model API, the person's data never leaving the laptop.
  • Background work: it acts in hidden windows without taking over the person's mouse or keyboard.
  • Proof: every result is checked, with an audit trail of what was done.

Who would pay. Two markets: individuals who want an assistant that learns their own tools, and companies with Windows software that has no API, where privacy and an audit trail matter more than speed. A model that fits this niche (a suggestion, never tested with customers): a free local core, paid team features, ready-made knowledge packs for common business software, and support.

Three engineering rules held throughout: nothing hardcoded to a particular application, no physical mouse or keyboard input, and no "done" without evidence.

2Market and competitors

Hojaiga overlapped with four kinds of products. Each covers part of the idea; none covered all four parts of the niche above.

WhoWhat they do wellWhere Hojaiga differed
HeyClicky (Clicky, by Farza)An AI teacher next to your cursor that sees the screen, talks and points at things; polished, fast, built on strong hosted models.Hojaiga's teaching layer aimed at the same experience on Windows with local models, and added doing the task itself with proof. On teaching, HeyClicky is the direct competitor and the better product.

Hosted computer-use agents from the major AI labsStrong general reasoning over screenshots.Cloud-first and paid per call; Hojaiga wanted local, private and verifiable.
Open research agents (Microsoft UFO and others)Windows multi-app agent designs.Research code; Hojaiga studied UFO's hand-off design and added scanning, proof and safety.

Credit. Clicky, by Farza, is an open-source AI teacher that lives next to the cursor, sees the screen, talks, and points at things (github.com/farzaa/clicky, MIT license; now HeyClicky). Hojaiga started in August 2026 as an automation system. In late September I studied Clicky's open-source code, and in October I built Hojaiga's teaching layer, called "Professor", for Windows with local models: see the screen, find every button, point at it and explain it. That part of Hojaiga is directly inspired by Clicky.

Other work that shaped the design: Microsoft's UFO (MIT), whose host-and-app-agent hand-off informed the multi-app "blackboard"; OmniParser's icon detector (MIT), used to find unlabelled icons; the Qwen3-VL model family for local vision; and the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark for honest grounding scores. Much of the code was typed with AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Gemini); the experiments and the measurements in this report come from runs on my own machine.

3The organ blueprint

The project began as a written specification before any code: an "automation operating system" made of organs, each with one job and a defined way of talking to the others, grouped in seven layers. The brain was to be a local LLM (Qwen3 through llama.cpp) with no cloud model behind it.

LayerOrgans in the blueprintWhat each was for
Core Intelligence01 Brain · 02 Central Nervous System · 03 Memorylocal reasoning and planning; the message bus that connects every organ; short- and long-term memory
Knowledge & Decision04 Knowledge · 05 Controllers · 06 Automationwhat the system knows about apps; turning plans into domain actions; driving windows, browsers and system dialogs
Execution07 Security · 08 Learning · 09 Infrastructurepermissions, secrets and risk; learning from outcomes; processes, storage and health
Platform10 Agents · 11 Interface · 12 Integrationspecialist agents; how people talk to it; connecting other tools
UI13 Interface layerthe visible assistant: overlay, voice, avatar
Runtime14 LLM runtimeloading and serving the local models on a 6 GB GPU
External15 External connectorsweb, files and outside services

In code the blueprint grew to more than sixty organ modules as problems appeared: a popup handler (29), an app scanner (30), a visual perception organ (31), a teaching organ (34), a task orchestrator (38), an app launcher (40), app intelligence (47), the behavior model that stores what each app does (48), a layout map of every control (50), a web layout organ (51), the model gateway (37) and app mastery (63), among others. Sections 4 to 6 describe what that system became and what it measurably did.

4Architecture as built

A task enters through one command and passes through six layers. Each layer can be tested on its own, and each reports what it did.

5Methods

5.1 Learning an app from its own files

Before a window ever opens, Hojaiga reads what the program ships with: menus, keyboard accelerators, dialogs and strings from the executable's resources; object models from type libraries (Excel: 746 objects and 13,896 members in 0.1 s); UI words from Store-app resource packages (Calculator: 1,166 words in 0.5 s); and strings and command lists from .NET and Electron apps. A sweep across the laptop found 196 real applications among 466 entries and extracted findings from 49 of them.

5.2 Mapping the live interface

The scanner walks the UI Automation tree in bulk (about ten times faster than one call per element), opens every menu, drop-down and safe dialog it can, records what each control leads to, and closes everything again. Controls that would change the person's data or start something (a slide show, a recording, a purchase) are refused by wording rules, never by app name. Where the tree is thin, a vision tier finds controls in the window's own pixels: on a synthetic test app it found 45 of 45 controls in light, dark, 125% and 150% scaling.

5.3 Acting without the person's mouse

Every action leaves through one actuation layer that picks a route per app family: UI Automation patterns, posted window messages, an in-process helper for apps that check the real cursor (WPF, Blender), or synthetic touch for WinUI. The person's cursor is never moved. Office apps are driven through their own object model in an invisible instance of their own, which is both faster and provable.

5.4 Proving results

A step passes only when its postcondition holds (the text is in the field, the dialog opened, the mode changed). A task passes only when its result is read back: the saved document, workbook or presentation is opened and checked against the request item by item, or the final window is described and judged by a vision model. This rule caught several false "done" reports during development, including leaky self-tests where the answer was hidden in the question.

5.5 Training local models

Qwen3-VL models were fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA on the 6 GB GPU: a 2B model on crawled click data, then a 4B model on a mixed set of 56,154 training rows from ten job types (point, read, ground, route, decide, judge, plan, teach, check, draw). Evaluation used 630 held-out items, including the public ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, with the answer never present in the prompt.

7What did not work, and why

These results matter as much as the ones above. They are the reason the project ends the way it does.

Test (held-out, 630 items)Base 4BFine-tuned 4B
All held-out rows53%39%
ScreenSpot-Pro (point inside the right box on pro-app screenshots)12.5%0%
Point at a control73%7%
Read a value off a screenshot90%17%
Choose the next action from a list50%73%
Safety traps (delete / send-all / admin)50%83%
  • Small models cannot be the eyes and the brain at once. On a 6 GB GPU the usable models are 2 to 8B parameters. The base 4B scored 12.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro. Fine-tuning on data that had only one answer shape made it better at choosing actions and much worse at seeing: it answered every pointing question with the centre of the screen.
  • Self-directed practice did not produce proven work. Across five overnight "learn this app" runs, the system mapped every app well but proved only 2 of the 100 tasks it set itself. Each run exposed a different gap in step execution (typing into an app with no text box, a check planned as an action, formatting words typed as text).
  • Modern apps resist structure. Store and WinUI apps (Calculator, Paint, Clock) often stop drawing their interface when hidden, menus close when the window loses focus, and Electron or Chromium apps expose a handful of nodes. Each needed its own workaround.
  • Drawing through a hidden window is fragile. Figure 4 shows a flowchart the system planned and what Paint actually received.

8Why I stopped

The core bet of Hojaiga was that it could have its own intelligence: local models plus knowledge it gathered itself, without paying for a large hosted model. The results above answer that bet. On the hardware an individual has (a 6 GB laptop GPU), models small enough to run locally could not see screens or plan reliably enough, and training them on my own data made the seeing worse. Every gain came from structure and verification, not from the local model getting smarter.

At the same time, the experience I most wanted people to have (an assistant that looks at your screen, points at the right button and explains it) already exists in HeyClicky, built on much larger models and done better. Competing with it would have meant using the same large models I had set out to avoid, and building the same product second.

So I made two decisions. First, finish Hojaiga in the form that works: keep the verified local core and let a large model teach it through the user's own API key, which section 9 describes. Second, publish everything, the code, the numbers and the failures, and move on to a new project.

9The exit build: a teacher and a brain

The structured core (knowledge from files, the verifier, the proof step, the safety gate) was sound. The weak part was the decision-maker. The last version keeps the local system in charge and adds a teacher it can consult:

The teacher runs on the user's own key, with a daily spending cap (two dollars by default) and a rule that prompts carrying credentials never leave the machine. The same model gateway also serves CrewAI agents, LangChain chains and ScrapeGraphAI web extraction, so every component shares one budget and one privacy rule. In the first live test a free hosted vision model chose the right control where the local brain had not, and the ledger recorded both answers and the proven outcome. The loop has 16 dedicated tests, all passing; it has not yet been run long enough to switch itself off, which needs at least 50 proven steps.

One licensing note for anyone continuing this: model providers' terms can restrict using their outputs to train competing models. The brain here learns by storing proven procedures and statistics, not by fine-tuning on teacher outputs; check the current terms before changing that.

10Safety and privacy

  • A consequence layer classifies every control and plan (money, publish, delete, account, install, settings) and asks before acting. Typed secrets are always blocked.
  • The assistant works in its own windows and closes only the processes it started, by process id. It never takes over an app the person already has open.
  • Screens are captured from the target window's own pixels, never as a screen grab, so other apps on the desktop are not recorded. Personal lists (recent files, signed-in names) are filtered out of the knowledge base.
  • No captchas, no account or IP rotation to get around rate limits, no credentials entered on anyone's behalf.

11Conclusion

Structure gives reliability, and proof gives honesty: those two ideas carried the project and are worth keeping. The idea that small local models could be the eyes and the brain of a general desktop assistant on a laptop did not hold up under held-out testing. The design that does hold up pairs a strong hosted teacher with a local system that checks, proves and remembers.

I am closing Hojaiga here and publishing it as a research release. The teaching experience I set out to build exists, and is done better, in HeyClicky. The code, the tests and the measurements are open for anyone who wants to continue the automation side.
